post.description:
Generate draft salary slips for a month, through a PayRun.

PAY-50 / PAY-17 — `/run` and `/calculate` produced structurally different
payslips from the same salary structure: `/run` summed the structure's
components with no statutory engine at all, and it is the path that writes
`SalarySlip`, the entity holding twelve months of history. It now opens (or
reuses) the PayRun for the month and delegates to `/calculate`, so there is
one builder, one answer per employee-month, and every slip carries its
`payrun_id` (LNK-19, DEMO-12).
Submit multiple salary slips at once.

Record the amount an approver allows AND take the Partially Approve edge.

MONEY-2026-09-16. `Partially Approve` was a bare transition: it takes no
fields, and a `submitted` claim refuses PUT, so the approved amount could
not be part of the decision and payroll paid the whole claim. The amount and
the state change are one decision, so they are one unit of work here: the
amount is written, then the ORDINARY transition endpoint runs with this
request — the caller's session roles, data scope and the flow's
`actor_not: created_by` all gate it exactly as they gate the button — and
any refusal rolls the amount back with it.

Calculate payroll for every employee on roll in a pay run's period.

PAY-14 — this route demanded only `PayRun:read` while it DELETEs and
rewrites every child row and overwrites the header totals a controller
already approved. It is a write, and is gated as one.

Calculate a leaver's full-and-final settlement.

PAY-28 — pressing Calculate silently DROPPED bonus, EPF settlement and the
other_earnings child array from gross, and forgave whatever sat in
other_deductions. Measured on the demo: Farida Sheikh's ₹297,576 became
₹108,000 — ₹189,576 removed from a payout — and a ₹4,500 canteen recovery
vanished. Every earning and deduction now goes through
`settlement_totals`, which reads all of them including the children.

PAY-29 — gratuity, notice pay and leave encashment were computed off CTC
with `basic = ctc_monthly * 0.5`, raw fractional service years, no ₹20L cap
and a hardcoded 15-day leave balance. Basic now comes from the employee's
salary structure, the years are rounded per s.4(2) of the Payment of
Gratuity Act, the cap applies, and the leave balance comes from
LeaveBalance when the tenant keeps one.

Statutory and payroll registers over a pay run, a period, or a fiscal year.

PAY-16 — this endpoint correctly joins Employee for UAN and ESI number and
had no caller in the application at all; the Reports screen dumped raw
PayRunEmployee rows instead, with eight columns bound to fields the entity
does not have (PAY-35). It now serves every statutory category the screen
offers, accepts a period rather than defaulting to the last 500 rows ever
written, and returns CSV when asked so the Download button can do something.

Server-side attendance counts for a period.

PAY-22 — the HR metrics bar and the dashboard pie computed the attendance
rate and the overtime total over whichever 500 rows the default sort
returned, with no date filter at all. A count-by-status aggregate cannot be
truncated by a page size.

PAY-21 — when the requested month has no rows, the response says which
month does, so the tiles can fall back rather than rendering "—" against
18,806 rows sitting in the table.

Live employee counts by department and designation.

PAY-23 — `Department.employee_count` and
`PayrollDesignation.employee_count` are stored, displayed in a column on
both screens, and never maintained: both read 0 for every row in a tenant
with 62 employees. Counting is a question, not a stored fact, so it is
answered here and the two screens read the answer.

Generate Form 16 Part B figures for a fiscal year.

PAY-9 — this summed every payslip ever recorded (the `fiscal_year`
parameter was accepted and never used), then multiplied an already-summed
TDS by twelve, and set `part_a_generated` and `part_b_generated` to True by
fiat. That is a fabricated statutory certificate. Now: payslips are
filtered to the FY's pay-run periods, the TDS is the sum and nothing else,
the deductor block comes from TaxConfig, the Chapter VI-A breakdown from
the employee's approved declarations, and Part A stays False because this
product does not hold TRACES challan data — the flag says what is true.

PAY-14 — gated on create of the entity it writes, not `PayRun:read`.

Generate the quarterly TDS return record for a quarter of a fiscal year.

PAY-10 — both `quarter` and `fiscal_year` were accepted and ignored, so
every quarter's record showed the same lifetime TDS number; there were no
deductee rows and no challans, so the record was not a return; and
Form24QRecord had no company_id, so on a multi-tenant instance every
tenant's returns commingled in one table with no way to scope them.

Report what the product can and cannot produce for a pay run's payslips.

PAY-45 — this returned `"status": "generated"` and rendered nothing. There
is no PDF renderer behind PayrollPDFTemplate, and a caller that believes
"generated" has no way to discover otherwise: the docstring said "(stub)"
and the JSON did not. It now answers honestly — the slips exist as records
and can be read or exported, the PDF is not implemented — and it stamps the
slips so the run and its payslips agree about state (PAY-47).

Report the payslip distribution list; do not claim mail that was not sent.

PAY-45 — this returned `"status": "sent"` and a recipient list, and nobody
received a payslip. Nothing is dispatched here because no payslip document
exists to attach (see generate_payslips); the route reports the recipients
it would use and says plainly that it sent nothing.

The NEFT/bulk-transfer advice for a pay run, as CSV.

PAY-46 — the final step of payroll, getting money to N bank accounts,
produced no file and no payment record; the bank picker in the wizard was
four hardcoded strings ("HSBC" offered to a tenant banking with ICICI) that
went nowhere, and PayrollBankAccount had no consumer at all. This emits the
advice from the run's own rows against the tenant's chosen
PayrollBankAccount, and refuses rather than emitting a half file when an
employee has no account number.
Always refuses with 501 and records `email_not_attempted`. Never sends.

Accepts `period` as `MM-YYYY` (what the screen sends and what the seeded
rows use), `Q<n>-YYYY` for a QRMP filer, or `FY<yyyy>-<yy>` for the annual
return; `from_date`/`to_date` remain accepted for API callers. A request

Reconcile GSTR-2B vendor filings against purchase records (Bills).

GST-13: matching was "same GSTIN, tax within one rupee" — the invoice
number was read out of the filing and used only to echo it back. A
supplier's filing could therefore be attributed to an arbitrary bill of
theirs, and on the demo it matched nothing at all because `bill.gst_no` is
NULL on all 18 rows. Matching now runs in three passes, strongest first,
and a bill is consumed once matched so one bill cannot satisfy two filings.

GST-14: `unmatched_bills` was initialised and never written to or returned
— and it is the half that matters most, because a purchase the supplier did
not file is ITC that must not be claimed.

Accept/reject/pending an IMS decision on inward documents.

GST-11: the screen posted `transaction_ids` and this read `bill_ids`, so
the loop body never ran and `{"ok": true, "updated": 0}` came back to a UI
that ignored the response and set the row from local React state. The
decision looked taken and was never stored. Both key names are accepted now
so neither side has to ship first.

GST-15: the UPDATE was `WHERE id = ?` with no tenant predicate — any row on
the deployment, by id.

Compute the tax rows for a document under the active tax regime.

Body: `{amount, party_id?, place_of_supply?/state_code?, county?, city?,
line1?, postal_code?, source_of_supply?, rate?/tax_id?, date?, lines?}`.
Returns `{taxes: [...]}` shaped for Invoice.taxes / Bill.taxes.

`lines` is optional and US-only:
`[{item_id?, item_code?, amount, quantity?, tax_code?, description?,
discount?}]`. Supplying it is what makes product taxability possible —
each line's tax code (its own, else `Item.tax_code`, else the configured
default) is sent to the provider, so groceries, clothing, prescription
drugs and SaaS are taxed the way the destination state actually taxes them
instead of all being treated as generic tangible personal property. Without
`lines` the behaviour is exactly what it was: one blended rate stack for the
ship-to address applied to `amount`.

Under `sales_use_tax` the response also carries `rate_source`,
`rate_source_status` and `rate_source_authoritative` — read those before
presenting the figure as filing-ready — plus `lines`, echoing the tax code
each line was sent with and where it came from. Under `gst` the source is
always `manual` (rates come from the Tax entity), no `lines` are read and
none are returned: that is the India demo path and it is untouched.

Statement of Cash Flows, indirect method.

Receivables aging by party: current / 1-30 / 31-60 / 61-90 / 91-120 / 120+.

Only `direction='receivable'` invoices are aged. `Invoice` holds both sides
of the ledger, so without that predicate every open supplier invoice is
reported as customer debt — on the Suryodaya seed that was 165 payables
worth ₹3.00 Cr inflating a ₹2.31 Cr receivables book to ₹5.31 Cr.

Under the GST regime the response also carries the MSME 45-day column
(`msme_breached` per party and in totals), so the same report serves the
Indian statutory question and the US A/R Aging Summary.

Payables aging by vendor, same buckets as AR.

Ages BOTH `Bill` and `Invoice(direction='payable')` — see `_merge_aging`.
A payable is a payable wherever it was entered, and reporting only one of
the two tables is how ₹3.00 Cr of the India tenant's book stayed off this
screen while counting towards the balance sheet's Accounts Payable.

This is where the MSME column matters most: §43B(h) disallows the deduction
when a registered micro/small vendor is paid later than 45 days from the
bill date, so `msme_breached` is the exposure figure.

Sales tax by jurisdiction, net of credit notes, with the ledger tie-out.

This is the US equivalent of the GSTR-1/3B screens and is gated on
`tax_regime == "sales_use_tax"`.

US-34. Three things were wrong and one was stale:

  * **credit notes were never read.** A return prepared from this report
    over-declared by every credit issued in the period, and there is no
    later correction — the number is what the state is told was collected.
  * **no cash basis.** Roughly half the states let a small seller file on
    cash receipts, and several require it. `?basis=cash` prorates each
    document's tax by how much of it was actually settled in the window.
  * **nothing tied to the ledger.** The figure a return is filed on has to
    be reconcilable to the movement in Sales Tax Payable, or an auditor
    cannot verify it and neither can the person signing the return.
    `ledger_reconciliation` does that, per jurisdiction where the
    jurisdiction names its own liability account (US-30).
  * the limitations block described a product that no longer exists: it
    said rates were manual with "no Avalara/TaxJar lookup" when the
    provider path had already shipped.

Get receivables/payables summary for a party.

BRINGUP-9: the gate named "Customer", and no such entity is registered —
the party model is `Party` and the money this route actually reads is
Invoice/Bill/CreditNote (below). `engine/permissions.py` returns early when
the schema lookup misses, so the gate passed everyone. It names `Invoice`
now: the strictest of the three entities it reads, and the one whose grants
already describe who may see a party's receivables. This is a real
tightening (role `user` is not granted Invoice read) — deliberate, because
a party's outstanding balance is finance data, and `finance_*` / `viewer`
keep it.

One party's ledger over a window, with an opening balance.

US-26 — three defects, all of which made this document wrong to send.
------------------------------------------------------------------
**No opening balance.** The running balance started at zero on `from`, so a
statement for "this quarter" opened at nil and its `closing_balance` was the
quarter's *movement* — not what the customer owes, which is the single
number the document exists to state.

**Receivables and payables in one list.** `Invoice` carries both directions
and the query filtered neither, and Bill / PaymentMade were appended to the
same array with the signs inverted. For a party who is both customer and
vendor — normal in manufacturing — the statement netted your purchases
against their debt and showed them your own supplier bills.

**Drafts included.** A document nobody has issued appeared on a statement
sent to a customer.

So: `?side=receivable` (default) or `?side=payable` picks one ledger,
`?include_opening=false` opts out of the pre-window query, and only posted
documents are listed. Both sides are still reachable — as two statements,
which is what they are.

post.description: Create a new @platform-domain email account.

§5.3.1 — the UNAUTHENTICATED public self-serve signup edge (R-11.1).

NO auth dependency: an anonymous visitor redeems an invite and, in one atomic
bootstrap, gets a Company + admin _users + UserCompany + seeded DomainConfig +
a live Stalwart mailbox on the shared public domain, then is logged in
(a session token, the register_user shape). The full abuse posture is layered
HERE: the invite gate (§4.2, inside bootstrap), the signup-rate limiter
(§4.3), the SelfServeSignup forensic ledger (every attempt), and the S04 spine
governing the new tenant's sends (§4.4, via the seeded DomainConfig).

Steps (§5.3.1):
  1. extract client IP (request.client.host — the /metrics / subscribe-form
     precedent) → check_signup_rate; on block return 429 + retry_after and
     write SelfServeSignup{rate_limited} (the limiter helper owns the bucket /
     WARN; this route owns the ledger row + the user-facing 429);
  2. validate password ≥ 8 (mirror api_rs_signup ~L2117);
  3. bootstrap_self_serve_tenant — on {error} map outcome → the right 4xx with
     a distinct user-facing reason (invite invalid/spent/email taken); the
     bootstrap already wrote its own SelfServeSignup row for that outcome;
  4. on success set the session token (return it like register_user does).

§11 instrumentation: self_serve_signups_total{outcome} on EVERY terminal path
+ self_serve_bootstrap_duration_seconds + a 5-key structured log. Secrets are
never logged.

SIGNUP-1 — the UNAUTHENTICATED INDIVIDUAL personal-signup edge (no invite).

The deliberate sibling of :func:`api_public_signup`: an anonymous visitor who
wants a personal mailbox on the shared public domain — NOT an organisation —
creates one WITHOUT an invite. This is the "there was no individual signup,
only Create Organisation" gap. The org-create edge (``/api/email/public-signup``)
stays invite-gated; this route is the separate, invite-FREE door so that gate
is never weakened.

Identical abuse posture to the invite edge — the SAME signup-rate limiter
(§4.3), the SAME password floor, the SAME STRICT verify-before-create gate
(S16 Phase D — a channel must be proven first), the SAME SelfServeSignup
forensic ledger, the SAME S04 spine governing the new tenant — MINUS the
invite gate. It calls ``bootstrap_personal_account`` (no invite consumed, no
invite redeemed) and, on success, logs the visitor in exactly like the invite
edge (a session token, the register_user shape).

get.description:
PUBLIC — resolve a live member invite to the new mailbox identity so the
activate screen can greet the member by address. 404 (no oracle) on any dead
token: unknown, expired, or already spent. Returns NO secret and NO token.

post.description:
PUBLIC — the invited member sets their OWN password. Drives the two-system
activation (Stalwart mailbox secret + _users bcrypt login hash), mints a
30-day session, and burns the single-use invite. Returns the signup shape
(auto-login). Maps the engine's ``{error, status}`` onto the HTTP status.

§5.3.2 — PLATFORM-operator invite issuance; plaintext shown ONCE.

BRINGUP-9 — why the second dependency exists. This route's own docstring
below calls issuance "a platform-operator action", and the schema comment
says the same, but `require_permission("SignupInvite", "create")` cannot
enforce it: `engine/permissions.py` short-circuits on `"admin" in roles`
before it ever reads the schema, and EVERY self-serve personal signup is
provisioned `role="admin"` of its own one-person org
(`self_serve.bootstrap_personal_account` → `hosting.provision_org_member`).
So the gate on the platform's invite-ONLY launch door (OD-4) was satisfied
by anyone who could pass an email OTP. Confirmed live against the bring-up
stack: an account created through the webmail's individual-signup form
minted a valid platform invite, with a caller-chosen `max_redemptions`, and
a DIFFERENT tenant's account then revoked it.

`require_platform_admin` is the same gate BRINGUP-8 put on `_roles`
mutation, for the same reason: a SignupInvite is anchored to the `'0'`
platform sentinel and bootstraps a tenant that does not exist yet, so
issuing one reaches outside any tenant an org admin owns.

Both dependencies are kept. The schema stays the source of truth for what
the entity's roles may do (rules §3) and answers 401 for an anonymous
caller under `REQUIRE_AUTH`; this one states the extra thing no schema can.
The operator's own path on a box with no platform account yet is
`scripts/mint_signup_invite.py`, which calls `issue_invite` in-process —
NOT an HTTP hole kept open for convenience.

The dedicated-route pattern the app_password.json _comment mandates (§4.2):
SignupInvite grants the user role NO generic-CRUD ([]), and the plaintext code
must never be re-fetchable, so issuance is a dedicated route — NOT generic
POST /api/SignupInvite. require_permission("SignupInvite","create") gates it
admin-only (the schema grants admin create). Calls issue_invite (which mints +
sha512_crypt-hashes the code, hash-only at rest — rules §7), returns the
plaintext code EXACTLY ONCE, and emits an AuditEvent on the '0' platform chain.

Body: {label (required), tier?, expires_at?, max_redemptions?}.

§5.3.2 — PLATFORM-operator invite revocation; sets revoked_at + audits.

Sets SignupInvite.revoked_at (the row is KEPT as the audit/forensics trail —
consume_invite rejects any invite with revoked_at set). Idempotent:
re-revoking an already-revoked invite is a 409 no-op (the SGA
approve-idempotency posture); a missing invite is a 404. Emits an AuditEvent
on the '0' platform chain.

below is deliberately un-scoped (`WHERE "id" = ?`, see the tenancy-lint note)
because an unredeemed invite owns no tenant to be scoped by. With `admin`
alone as the gate, that made every invite on the platform revocable by any

signup revoked a DIFFERENT tenant's invite. Ids are uuid4 and the generic
`GET /api/SignupInvite` is already scoped away from the '0' chain, so this
was reach over a known id rather than an enumeration — but "you need the id
first" is not an authorization control.

A sender asks for human re-examination of a content-blocked send (§5.8.4).

The compose surface's content-block banner ("Request review" button) POSTs
``{message_id, reason_code}``. ``message_id`` is the blocked draft id — the
same value ``outbound_filter`` stamped on ``OutboundBlockEvent.message_draft_id``
when it persisted the block. We flip the tenant's matching ``blocked`` event
to ``status='review_requested'`` so it surfaces in the operator moderation
queue (the ``status`` field IS the queue — no separate entity).

This is NOT a self-clear: a user can never reach ``approved``/``dismissed``
(those stay admin-only via the ``/approve`` endpoint), they only raise a
hand. So it is gated on the user's ``OutboundBlockEvent.read`` permission,
not admin write. Tenant-scoped to ``request.state.company_id`` — a caller
can only request review on a block in their own tenant. Idempotent: a block
already ``review_requested`` returns 200; a terminal block returns 409.

Senior/operator-only: `OutboundBlockEvent.write` is admin-only in the schema
(users may READ their own blocks but never self-clear — approval mirrors the
§5.13 abuse desk). Flow:

  1. Tenant-gate the block (404 cross-tenant / missing).
  2. Only `blocked` / `review_requested` can be approved (409 otherwise —
     already approved/dismissed is terminal + idempotent-safe).
  3. Flip `status → approved`, stamp `reviewed_by` / `reviewed_at` /
     `review_notes`, and write a durable `_audit_log` transition row.
  4. RE-QUEUE the held draft: if `message_draft_id` points at a live
     EmailMessage, set it `status='queued', folder='outbox',
     scheduled_send_at=now` so the background outbound loop dispatches it.
     The re-dispatch re-runs suppression + kill only — content is NOT
     re-scanned (the operator's approval IS the override, §5(c)).

`data.review_notes` (optional) is recorded on the decision.

  * `cohort`           — the named cohort the assignment is warming in.
  * `daily_cap`        — the pool's CURRENT ramp tier.
  * `top_tier`         — the top of `daily_cap_schedule` (graduation cap).
  * `days_to_graduation` — remaining tiers above the current cap. The daily
    promote_ip_pool action advances ~one tier per clean day, so the count of
    remaining tiers is the optimistic days-to-graduation; 0 = at top tier

post.description:

Idempotent (re-running lands the same state) and TENANT-SCOPED (the scan and every
mutation bind ``AND company_id = ?`` to the session tenant). Actions apply to the
MATCHED MESSAGES only, never to non-matching siblings in the same conversation.

``delete`` moves matched messages to Trash — a soft move, not a hard delete — but
once in Trash they follow the tenant's Trash-retention policy (which for old mail
purges relatively soon), so this is 'reversible for a while', not forever. A stale
condition whose field is blank/unknown is DROPPED (never treated as match-all), and
``forward-to`` / ``redirect`` / ``snooze-until`` are SKIPPED (a retroactive re-send
or snooze is unsafe/meaningless) and reported in ``skipped_actions``.

Atomicity: the multi-UPDATE mutation path is not wrapped in one transaction (the db
layer autocommits per statement); a mid-run fault can leave a thread's folder briefly
out of step with its messages, which a re-run (idempotent) reconciles.

Returns ``{matched, scanned, truncated, applied: {moved/trashed/marked_read/starred/
labeled}, skipped_actions}``.

put.description:
SHARE-25: this route had NO authorization of any kind.

`require_write_scope(request)` answers "does this caller belong to a
workspace" — which is a tenancy question, not a permission one. So any
authenticated user with a company (a viewer, a student, any role) could
overwrite the custom-field values on ANY record in their workspace: deals,
invoices, patient records. Custom fields are ordinary business data — on a
clinic or an HR deployment they are the sensitive half of the record — and
nothing asked whether the caller may write the entity they name.

It also created value rows against ids that do not exist, so the table
accumulated orphans addressed by a type/id pair nobody could ever reach.

Two checks, in this order:
  * `check_permission(request, entity_type, "write")` — the TARGET entity's
    own declaration. Writing a custom field on an Invoice is writing an
    Invoice; it may not answer a question `PUT /api/Invoice/{id}` refuses.
  * the record must exist INSIDE the caller's scope. `scope_sql` renders the
    same Layer-3 decision the generic CRUD path binds, so a record in
    another tenant is not found rather than being written to.

`entity_type` reaches SQL only as a bound parameter here, but it is resolved
through the registry first anyway — an unregistered name now 404s instead of
silently creating a row against a table that does not exist.

MX-38 — remove a compose-tray upload nothing references.

`POST /api/upload` had no counterpart. Attach a 25 MB file, change your mind,
and it stayed on disk — reachable at its `/uploads/<uuid>` URL, because that
path is a bare StaticFiles mount — for the life of the box. The nightly
sweep (`scripts/sweep_orphan_uploads.py`) reclaims it a day later; this is
the immediate half, called when the composer removes an attachment from the
tray or discards a draft.

Two guards, in this order:

  * the name must resolve to a DIRECT CHILD of the upload root. Traversal,
    an absolute path and a nested `drive/<file>` are all refused — Drive's
    files belong to FileAttachment rows and are deleted through Drive;
  * it must not be referenced. This route has no age floor to hide behind,
    so it consults the SAME rule the sweep uses
    (`engine.email.upload_refs`), which fails CLOSED: deleting a file a
    queued send-later message still names would send an empty attachment.

A file that is already gone answers 200. The caller's intent — "this should
not exist" — is satisfied, and a 404 would make the composer's cleanup noisy
for a race it cannot win.

post.description:
Carry out one data-subject request: export the package, or apply the decision.

`action: "export"` assembles the package and records its digest. It changes
no contact and deletes nothing.

`action: "apply"` runs the SAME discovery the detail screen showed and then
does exactly one of three things:

  * **refuses**, when any Party-linked source was unreadable. A discovery
    with a denied source cannot support a claim of complete erasure, and
    saying so is the only honest answer;
  * **restricts**, when a statutory retention obligation holds any record.
    The contact is marked `restricted`, which makes
    `engine/contacts/consent.py::evaluate_communication_eligibility` fail
    closed for marketing immediately — so the restriction reaches the
    campaign sender rather than being a label on a screen — and the receipt
    carries the earliest date erasure becomes possible;
  * **erases**, when nothing holds it: the Party's identifying fields are
    replaced with a visible tombstone.

IT NEVER DELETES A RELATED RECORD. An invoice with no counterparty is not a
repaired record, it is a broken one, and destroying books of account is the
unlawful act rather than the lawful one. Identity lives on `Party`; the
entities that keep their own copy of a name or an address are counted and
NAMED in the receipt under `unreached_codes` instead of being quietly left
behind.

plugin one tenant asked for appeared in every other tenant's sidebar and its
endpoints went live for all of them. Enabling is now two statements that
must both hold —

  * the plugin-wide `status` says the code is LOADED in the process (this
    route still sets it, and it is still a platform act: plugin code is

for every tenant by design, so it takes no `company_id` and only the
platform grain — already the gate on this whole router — can enable it.

`company_id` defaults to the caller's own tenant (a platform operator who
has switched into a workspace, ADR-006 §2.2.4). A per-tenant plugin with no
tenant to name is REFUSED rather than enabled everywhere, which is the
behaviour this finding is about.

get.description: List installed modules with canonical catalogue metadata.

Return MCP-compatible tool definitions for the entire platform.

RT-6. This was fully anonymous; wave 1 put `_require_session` on it, which
closed the stranger and nothing else. What it returns is the complete
reconnaissance map of the deployment — every entity, every engine script,
every declared action and every module endpoint — which is precisely the
menu an attacker needs to aim RT-2's action steps and the script runner.
Any `user`-role account still got the whole thing, and under
`REQUIRE_AUTH=false` it was open again.

THE FLOOR IS NOW THE CALLER'S OWN ENTITLEMENTS, NOT THE PLATFORM GRAIN.

The reasoning above was right about the danger and wrong about the remedy.
An unscoped catalogue IS a reconnaissance map, so it was hidden behind
`require_admin_floor` — the platform grain. But that locked out the people
the surface exists for: measured on the live deployment, the TENANT admin
got 403, so an admin/EA agent could not list a single tool. And because
`generate_mcp_tools` returns `[]` unless `allow_unmounted=True`, even a
platform operator got an empty list. The route was shut to everyone.

The fix is to scope the catalogue rather than hide it. Passing `request`
makes `engine/mcp.py` filter every tool through the SAME predicates in
engine/permissions.py that decide the REST answer — Layer 1 roles, Layer 2
`allowed_apps` (with `core` exempt), Layer 3 row scope, plus each app's
declared `mcp_exposure`. A tool the caller may not use is ABSENT, not merely
refused on call, so the map itself is scoped: a tenant admin sees the whole
tenant (2,660 tools measured), a seat sees only its own apps' (127-296), and
`action.*` and bare `script.*` reach nobody — api-actions run outside the
permission layer and 92 scripts hold raw cross-tenant SQL.

`_require_session` still refuses the stranger, which was wave 1's correct
